#9815. MLOps: models that survive production · 4. Reproducible training pipelines

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at amitchakraborty.dev

MLOps: models that survive production · Chapter 4 of 12 · AI Engineering · new chapter every Thursday night

By the end of this chapter: Turn a notebook into something that runs unattended.

Say you are a machine learning engineer who has spent weeks perfecting a model in a Jupyter notebook. You have tuned the hyperparameters, selected the best features, and achieved impressive accuracy on your training data. However, when you try to deploy the model to a production environment, you realize that the model is not reproducible. The accuracy drops significantly, and you are unable to understand why. You have tried to recreate the exact same environment, but it seems like the model is sensitive to some unknown factor. This has cost you several days of debugging, and you are starting to worry that you will miss your deployment deadline.

You are not alone in this struggle. Many machine learning engineers face the same issue when trying to deploy their models to production. The problem lies in the fact that Jupyter notebooks are designed for exploration, not execution. They hide the complexity of state, time, and data distribution, making it difficult to reproduce the exact same conditions in a production environment.

In your case, the symptom is a significant drop in accuracy when deploying the model to production. The metric that has moved is the model's accuracy, which has decreased from 99% in the notebook to 80% in production. This has cost you time, as you have had to spend several days debugging the issue, and it has also cost you sleep, as you are worried about missing your deployment deadline.

To follow along with this chapter, you will need to have Python 3.8 or later installed, as well as the pip package manager. You should also have a basic understanding of machine learning concepts and experience with Jupyter notebooks. If you have not already, install the required packages by running the following command:

Verify that the installation was successful by running:

If you do not see any errors, you are ready to proceed.

To create a reproducible training pipeline, we need to address the issues that make Jupyter notebooks non-reproducible. One of the main issues is the lack of control over the environment. To mitigate this, we can use a tool like conda to create a reproducible environment.

Create a new conda environment using the following command:

This will create a new environment named myenv with Python 3.8 installed.

Activate the environment using the following command:

This will activate the myenv environment, and you should see the name of the environment printed on your command line.

Install the required packages using the following command:

This will install the required packages, including scikit-learn, pandas, and numpy.

Create a new Python script called train.py with the following content:

This script loads the data, splits it into training and testing sets, trains a random forest classifier, and evaluates its accuracy.

To build the reproducible training pipeline, follow these steps:

This file defines the conda environment required for your project.

This will train the model and print its accuracy to the console.

One common issue that can occur when building a reproducible training pipeline is that the environment is not properly activated. If you see an error message indicating that a package is not installed, it may be because the environment is not activated. To fix this, simply activate the environment using the conda activate command.

Another issue that can occur is that the data is not properly loaded. If you see an error message indicating that the data file is not found, it may be because the file path is incorrect. To fix this, simply update the file path in the train.py script to point to the correct location of the data file.

The approach outlined in this chapter has several costs associated with it. One of the main costs is the time required to set up the conda environment and install the required packages. This can take several minutes, depending on the speed of your internet connection and the size of the packages.

Another cost is the disk space required to store the environment and the data. This can be significant, depending on the size of the data and the number of packages installed.

Finally, there is a cost associated with maintaining the environment over time. As new packages are released, you will need to update the environment to ensure that you have the latest versions. This can be time-consuming, especially if you have multiple environments to maintain.

In an interview, you may be asked to explain how you would create a reproducible training pipeline. A weak answer might focus on the technical details of the pipeline, without considering the broader context of the project. For example, a candidate might say something like:

"I would use conda to create a reproducible environment, and then install the required packages using pip."

A stronger answer would consider the trade-offs involved in creating a reproducible pipeline, and explain how the approach would be tailored to the specific needs of the project. For example:

"I would use conda to create a reproducible environment, but I would also consider the cost of setting up and maintaining the environment over time. I would weigh the benefits of using a cloud-based environment against the costs of setting up and maintaining a local environment. I would also consider the trade-offs involved in using a pre-built environment versus building a custom environment from scratch."

As a senior engineer, you might be expected to explain how you would scale the approach to a large team, and how you would ensure that the pipeline is maintainable and efficient over time. For example:

"I would use a combination of conda and Docker to create a reproducible environment that can be easily scaled to a large team. I would also use a continuous integration pipeline to automate the testing and deployment of the model, and ensure that the environment is properly maintained and updated over time."

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

#9813. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

Sounds Good So let’s start

What is CJ Affiliate?

Commission Junction is an online advertising company that offers affiliate programs for various retailers. Since 1998, it has been known as one of the oldest and most popular affiliate networks. 

 Commission Junction has consistently ranked among the top 10 affiliate networks 

With in-depth data analysis and an unmatched understanding of clients needs, CJ has established itself as a leader in performance marketing.

CJ provides advertisers with a variety of tracking, management, and payment options. As an affiliate network, CJ can help you launch multiple affiliate programs from a centralized network.

Requirements

How Does CJ Affiliate Work?

#9811. Initialize Once, Hydrate Deliberately: Choosing a FeatureCell's Starting State

Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at sdux-vault.com

A FeatureCell does not start with "whatever was in the constructor." Calling initialize() activates the runtime pipeline, and the value it begins with depends on a resolved decision between a declared default, a previously persisted value, and a deliberate hydrate() factory. Knowing which source wins — and why — is what separates an accidental starting value from an intentional one.

This post walks through what initialize() actually activates, when hydrate() overrides everything else, and how to choose between a static default, Persist behaviors, and an explicit factory when your FeatureCell comes online.

Key takeaway: Initialization is not a direct mutation. Whatever value is selected — hydrated, persisted, or declared — is enqueued as a replaceState operation and processed through the same pipeline as any other update.

A FeatureCell is not operational the moment it is declared. It becomes a runtime participant only after initialize() is called — once, and exactly once. Reading state, issuing updates, or interacting with a FeatureCell before initialization results in a runtime error, and calling initialize() a second time does the same.

That boundary matters because initialization is where configuration becomes behavior. Filters, reducers, taps, error handlers, and emit configuration all have to be declared on the fluent builder before initialize() runs. Once initialization completes, the pipeline is fixed for the lifetime of that FeatureCell.

Calling initialize() transitions a FeatureCell from a configured definition into an active runtime participant. In order, it validates the declared configuration and behaviors, registers the FeatureCell with the Vault runtime, activates the Conductor execution surface, evaluates whichever initialization source was declared, and — if that source produced a value — enqueues it as the first replaceState operation.

If no initialization mechanism is declared at all, the FeatureCell still becomes active, but with value: undefined, waiting for an explicit replaceState() call. Declaring a default is optional; becoming active is not.

Here, descriptor.initialState is the only declared source, so that array becomes the first candidate through Resolve, Filters, Reducers, and Emit — the same pipeline any later update travels through.

During initialization, Vault evaluates exactly one initialization source, in strict precedence order:

These are not fallback layers. Vault does not try hydrate(), fail, and then fall back to Persist or the descriptor. Only the single highest-precedence declared source is evaluated at all.

hydrate(factory) registers a deferred factory that does not run when it is called — it runs only when initialize() runs. The factory may return a value synchronously, return a Promise, resolve to undefined, or throw. When declared, it overrides both Persist behaviors and descriptor.initialState outright, because declaring hydrate() is an explicit statement that persisted or static data should not be treated as authoritative for this initialization cycle.

⚠️ Warning: That descriptor still declares initialState: [], but once hydrate() is registered, it is never evaluated. Declaring both is not a layering strategy — only one source wins.

The practical question at startup is simple: should this FeatureCell begin with a declared default, a persisted value, or an explicit factory? Each source answers a different need.

Persisted storage can go stale the moment the underlying data changes elsewhere, and a static descriptor is static by definition. hydrate() exists for the case where neither of those should be treated as authoritative — if dynamic resolution is not actually needed, do not declare it, and Vault evaluates storage or the descriptor according to precedence instead.

A deferred factory does not always resolve the way you expect, and hydrate() treats "no value" very differently from "something went wrong."

An undefined result is not treated as a failure — it just means nothing committed. A thrown error or rejected Promise is treated as a failure, because the declared authoritative source did not resolve the way the application promised it would.

If that fetch rejects, initialization fails: hasValue stays false, value stays undefined, and error is populated. The pipeline keeps running — it does not crash the application — but nothing committed as declared. Recovery, if you want it, has to be explicit, using reset() and replaceState() to put the FeatureCell into a known state on your own terms.

⚠️ Warning: If hydrate() throws, Vault does not quietly drop down to Persist behaviors or descriptor.initialState. The FeatureCell does not activate partially, and the failure is visible instead of masked.

A live, interactive StackBlitz demo of hydrate() overriding a descriptor default is available on the original article if you want to try the sequence yourself.

Read the full method contracts for initialize() and hydrate() in the FeatureCell API reference, including the full precedence rules, diagrams, and resolution outcome tables this post draws from.

#9808. Building a Multi-Agent Website Launch Validator With OpenMinion

Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.

Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.

Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.

I run a small web agency. We build and host websites for small businesses in the US and Brazil, and every launch has the same floor: a title and a description, a canonical URL, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, icons, a sitemap, a 404 page that really returns 404, an llms.txt, and a robots.txt that does not lock AI search crawlers out. For years we checked that list by hand, one tab per item.

For Cortensor Hackathon 5, I turned the checklist into an agent called Go-Live Gate, built on OpenMinion 0.1, the agent SDK from the Cortensor ecosystem. It answers one question: is this site ready, ready with warnings, or blocked? The code is MIT-licensed at github.com/DesignMaster-Solutions/golive-gate and there is a 2-minute demo at youtu.be/tVH-x62QV3I.

This post is about the one design decision that made it trustworthy, and about what it looks like to run an agent on open, swappable inference instead of one vendor's API.

The tempting version of this agent is one prompt: "here is a URL, tell me if it is ready". That version hallucinates. It will tell you a sitemap exists because sites usually have one.

So Go-Live Gate is split in three agents with different powers:

Every run writes facts.json next to report.md. A reviewer can open both and check the model's verdict against what the tools actually saw. That file is the whole point: the agent is only as honest as the layer under it, and that layer has its own offline tests against a local HTTP server.

When the facts live in code and the model only reasons over them, the model becomes replaceable. That is what makes open inference practical for a business tool.

OpenMinion talks to any OpenAI-compatible provider. Our recorded runs used a free open-weight model (nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free through OpenRouter); the same project is set up for the Cortensor Portal with one command (setup --provider cortensor-portal). I did not have to rewrite prompts or tools to switch. The judge's output is validated by a schema either way, so a weaker or slower node fails loudly instead of quietly writing a wrong verdict.

If you are building on a decentralized inference network, you cannot assume the same model, the same latency or the same token limits on every call. Designing the agent so that the model is the least trusted part is how you get repeatable results anyway.

The hackathon asked for building blocks tested and lessons learned, and these were the useful ones:

And one bug was mine. The first live run flagged a 697-character title on a client site whose real title is 63 characters. My parser was concatenating the elements inside inline SVG icons. The agent repeated what the tool reported, which is exactly why the facts layer has regression tests and the model does not get the last word.</p> <p>On capegraniteconnection.com, a site we built, the gate returned ready with 11 checks: title 63 characters, description 149, canonical present, all four Open Graph tags, 12 JSON-LD types including LocalBusiness and FAQPage, en-US, both icons, no AI crawler blocked, a sitemap with 44 URLs, a 3,902-byte llms.txt, and a real 404. On a free model the investigator took 232 seconds and the judge 355. Slow, but it runs unattended before every launch, and it is cheaper than the hour of tabs it replaces.</p> <p>The lesson I would carry to any agent on open infrastructure: let code collect the facts, let the model reason over them, put a schema on the answer and a human in front of anything that writes. Then the model can come from anywhere.</p> <p>Founder of Design Master Solutions. I build websites, apps and AI agents for small businesses in the US and Brazil.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://hackernoon.com/building-a-multi-agent-website-launch-validator-with-openminion?source=rss" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9807"> <h2>#9807. Node.js Compresses AI-Generated Images for Cloud Upload: Replaying Tenant Retention</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fiz24db5986namaa4tl8u.png" alt="Node.js Compresses AI-Generated Images for Cloud Upload: Replaying Tenant Retention" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>For a game studio storing AI-generated training images, the difficult question is not how to upload bytes. It is how to prove, six months later, why an artifact still exists, which tenant owns it, and which retention rule produced that outcome.</p> <p>Short answer: compress the image with Sharp, derive the object key from validated tenant and job identifiers, keep the object private, and persist the policy version beside the upload record. Replaying the same policy inputs should produce the same retention decision. The storage API is replaceable; that record is the governance boundary.</p> <p>Infrai is a practical fit when this worker needs one REST API and one credential across backend capabilities, without installing a storage SDK. The upload contract can stay stable while the supported storage vendor behind it changes.</p> <p>The before-and-after model is simple. Before, a cleanup task sees renders/final.webp and guesses. After, it sees tenant_42/training/2026-10/policy-3/job_8f2/image.webp, plus a record saying which policy version created it. The path is not an access-control system, but it makes an accidental cross-tenant reference much easier to detect.</p> <p>Start with inputs, not a deletion date. For each generated image, store the tenant ID, training job ID, policy version, retention duration, object key, output format, byte count, and creation timestamp. Store the decision status too: eligible, held, or deleted. A worker can then recompute eligibility without inspecting pixels or relying on a mutable filename.</p> <p>This is a useful distinction. A lifecycle rule is an execution mechanism. The policy record is the explanation.</p> <p>Use a deterministic key convention, but do not treat it as a substitute for authorization. Validate tenant and job identifiers before interpolating them. Keep the bucket name configured by the deployment, not supplied by an end user. A private object and a signed URL for a reviewer preserve a much narrower access boundary than a permanent public link.</p> <p>I initially treated compression as a storage concern only. That misses the operational part. A 12 MB source that becomes a 900 KB WebP is faster to retry, cheaper to move through a worker, and less burdensome for a later review tool. The byte count belongs in the policy record because it describes the workload that the retention process actually handled.</p> <p>The example below keeps the image transformation and the write in one worker function. It uses an explicit PUT, a tenant-scoped key, a private ACL header, and an idempotency key derived from the immutable job identity. The endpoint is the only storage route in the example.</p> <p>The database write should use the same job identity as the upload record. On a retry, the worker reuses the idempotency key rather than creating a second logical artifact. A 429 gets a bounded exponential delay, and Retry-After wins when the server supplies it. Those two details are small, but they make the audit trail line up with actual write attempts.</p> <p>The policy record is the part worth reviewing in an architecture meeting. Imagine a training job created on October 24 with policy version 3 and a 30-day hold. If the retention rule changes to 90 days on October 30, the old artifact still carries version 3; a replay can evaluate it under the rule that created it instead of silently applying the latest rule. That is why the month, policy version, and job ID appear in the key, while the database retains the complete inputs. The key helps a human spot scope. The record makes the decision reproducible.</p> <p>Do not place a bearer token on a returned presigned URL. The signed URL is a separate access request. The upload worker owns the authenticated write; a reviewer gets the narrow read path your access policy permits.</p> <p>For larger images, move this function behind a queue worker. The request that starts a generation job should record the job ID and return. It should not keep a game-facing request open while Sharp transforms and uploads a whole batch.</p> <p>Amazon S3 is the reference point for provider-native governance. Teams already using AWS identity, bucket policy, lifecycle controls, and object tooling may value that depth more than a uniform abstraction. The trade-off is that the application inherits AWS-specific configuration and operational vocabulary.</p> <p>Cloudflare R2 is a reasonable option for a studio already operating at Cloudflare’s edge and using an S3-compatible object interface. It can fit delivery-oriented workloads, but the team still needs to validate the exact access and lifecycle behavior it depends on.</p> <p>Alibaba Cloud OSS is relevant when the studio’s regions, identity model, or existing data estate are centered on Alibaba Cloud. It is a better fit than a neutral gateway when OSS-native administration and vendor controls are the governing requirement.</p> <p>Infrai fits a different governance question. Its storage surface covers supported vendors including R2, S3, OSS, and COS, while the application keeps one plain REST upload contract. In this workflow, that means the worker’s policy and key logic can stay put when the backend vendor changes; the contract remains stable while the thing behind it moves. The API is also self-describing through a public discovery surface, and its documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, which makes a small TypeScript worker easier to inspect and port.</p> <p>That is a concrete recommendation, not a universal one: try Infrai for private, tenant-scoped training artifacts when keeping the upload contract stable is more important than exposing every provider-native governance control directly in application code. Choose S3, R2, or OSS when their native policy, region, or delivery features are themselves the requirement.</p> <p>The boundary matters more than the abstraction. This storage surface has no public or public-read ACL, so public_url remains null. It is not suitable for a static website, a permanent public image link, or a general image host. Use a distribution service designed for public delivery.</p> <p>There is no object versioning or object lock. An accidental overwrite cannot be recovered through those mechanisms, and a financial-grade WORM archive needs an external design. There is also no If-Match conditional write. If two workers must be mutually exclusive, make the claim in a queue or database before the upload.</p> <p>Browser-direct upload needs care. There is no independently exposed set_cors route for self-service configuration, so a frontend should not assume it can configure cross-origin uploads through this storage surface. A trusted worker is the simpler boundary for this training-artifact workflow.</p> <p>Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum. Multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix filtering, and there is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Supported vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS, not GCS or B2. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes.</p> <p>Those are selection criteria, not footnotes. If the artifact needs immutable retention, public distribution, browser-managed CORS, or cross-region recovery, a specialist provider or an external control plane is the better choice.</p> <p>If this boundary fits your system, start with the Node.js Sharp storage upload guide and verify the bucket and access policy before wiring the worker into production.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/horatiofox1281/nodejs-compresses-ai-generated-images-for-cloud-upload-replaying-tenant-retention-439c" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9806"> <h2>#9806. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/sites/default/files/2026-09/400968%20Baker%27s%20Reserve%20Bread%20Flour_Spring%20Lifestyle%20Direct_2027_Shot%201_H_2674.jpg" alt="What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour." style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.</p> <p>The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.</p> <p>To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.</p> <p>High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.</p> <p>High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.</p> <p>You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.</p> <p>Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.</p> <p>If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.</p> <p>Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.</p> <p>Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.</p> <p>Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.</p> <p>Cover photo by Patrick Marinello; food styling by Yekaterina Boytsova.</p> <p>Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.</p> <p>Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.</p> <p>See our complete collection of Story posts.</p> <p>Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.</p> <p>Don’t fall for this classic sourdough starter trick.</p> <p>Facebook TikTok Instagram Threads Pinterest LinkedIn YouTube Reddit Substack</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/blog/2026/09/28/what-is-high-extraction-flour" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9805"> <h2>#9805. Measuring the Impact of EAS Builds and OTA Updates</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fxrxvrrwrlpyszlrwxgkk.supabase.co%2Fstorage%2Fv1%2Fobject%2Fpublic%2Fproject-images%2Fblog%2Feas-builds-and-ota-updates-measuring-before-optimising.jpg" alt="Measuring the Impact of EAS Builds and OTA Updates" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at amitchakraborty.dev</p> <p>Say you are a mobile developer tasked with optimizing the performance of your React Native application. You've heard that using EAS builds and OTA updates can improve the user experience, but you're not sure where to start or how to measure the impact of these changes. You're about to embark on a potentially time-consuming rewrite, and you want to know whether it's worth it.</p> <p>You're trying to improve the performance of your React Native application, and you've identified EAS builds and OTA updates as potential areas for optimization. However, you're not sure how to measure the current performance of your app, or how to determine whether the rewrite will have a significant impact. You've tried using various metrics, such as app launch time and battery usage, but you're not sure which ones are most relevant or how to collect accurate data.</p> <p>EAS builds and OTA updates can have a significant impact on the performance of a React Native application, but measuring this impact can be challenging. One of the main reasons is that there are many factors that can affect performance, such as network connectivity, device hardware, and user behavior. Additionally, the metrics that are typically used to measure performance, such as app launch time and battery usage, may not be directly related to the changes made during the rewrite. To make matters worse, the documentation for EAS builds and OTA updates often focuses on the features and functionality, rather than the performance implications.</p> <p>To measure the impact of EAS builds and OTA updates, you'll need to instrument your application to collect relevant metrics. Here are the steps to follow:</p> <p>Measuring the impact of EAS builds and OTA updates can be time-consuming and may require significant resources, especially if you're using a third-party instrumentation tool. However, the cost of not measuring the impact can be even higher, as you may end up making changes that don't have a significant effect on performance. Consider the following trade-offs:</p> <p>When interviewing a candidate for a mobile development position, you may ask questions like:</p> <p>Amit Chakraborty is a founding engineer and senior architect — React Native, AI/RAG systems and production architecture. Neura HQ</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><p> The agentic conversational storefront for consumer brands </p> <p> <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/products/neura-4?utm_campaign=producthunt-atom-posts-feed&utm_medium=rss-feed&utm_source=producthunt-atom-posts-feed">Discussion</a> | <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/r/p/1304141?app_id=339">Link</a> </p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.producthunt.com/products/neura-4" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9800"> <h2>#9800. Sparen of beleggen: waar groeit je geld het hardst?</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F6vhmw1h0yshe5iefffvi.png" alt="Sparen of beleggen: waar groeit je geld het hardst?" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Bij ons thuis werd sparen vroeger besproken alsof het een deugd was — en beleggen alsof het een gok was. Mijn ouders hadden hun geld op een spaarrekening, punt. Dat stond veilig, dat kon je zien groeien, en daar sliep je goed van. Ik heb dat lang klakkeloos overgenomen, tot ik een keer naast elkaar uitrekende wat honderd euro per maand doet op een spaarrekening versus in een gespreide belegging. Het verschil was zo groot dat ik mijn ouders er bijna over belde. Bijna — want het eerlijke verhaal is genuanceerder dan "beleggen wint". Laten we het goed uitrekenen, met de voor- én nadelen erbij.</p> <p>Eerst het sparen. Je zet €100 per maand op een rekening met 2% rente, maandelijks bijgeschreven. Na twintig jaar staat er €29.529 — zelf heb je €24.000 ingelegd, dus de rente heeft er zo'n €5.529 bij gedaan. Dat is precies wat sparen belooft: voorspelbaar, rustig, en je geld is er als je het nodig hebt. Er valt geen maand tussen waarin je saldo ineens tien procent lager staat. Voor geld dat je binnen nu en een paar jaar nodig hebt — een auto, een aanbetaling, een buffer — is dat niet alleen verstandig, dat is de enige juiste keuze.</p> <p>Dan het beleggen, met dezelfde honderd euro per maand. Tegen 5% gemiddeld rendement heb je na twintig jaar €41.275. Tegen 7% is het €52.397. Zelfde inleg van €24.000, maar het rendement is dan respectievelijk €17.275 of €28.397 — tegenover die €5.529 van de spaarrekening. En hoe langer je het laat staan, hoe schever de verhouding wordt. Na dertig jaar: sparen tegen 2% geeft €49.355 van je €36.000 inleg, terwijl 7% uitkomt op €122.709. Meer dan twee keer zoveel eindkapitaal uit exact hetzelfde maandbedrag. De regel van 72 verklaart waarom: deel 72 door je rendement en je hebt de verdubbelingstijd. Bij 2% duurt verdubbelen zo'n 36 jaar, bij 7% ongeveer 10 jaar. De belegger ziet zijn geld in dezelfde periode dus ruim drie keer verdubbelen waar de spaarder nog op zijn eerste verdubbeling wacht.</p> <p>Er is nog een onzichtbare tegenstander die vooral spaarders raakt: inflatie. Geld dat stilstaat, verliest koopkracht. Reken maar mee: €100.000 dat dertig jaar blijft liggen, is bij 2% inflatie in koopkracht van nu nog maar ongeveer €55.000 waard. Je saldo lijkt gelijk, maar je kunt er bijna de helft minder mee kopen. Bij een spaarrente van 2% en inflatie van 2% ren je dus op een loopband: je cijfer groeit, je werkelijke vermogen niet. Dat betekent niet dat sparen zinloos is — het betekent dat sparen een ander doel dient dan groeien.</p> <p>Want nu de eerlijke keerzijde van beleggen, want die hoort er net zo hard bij. Die 5% en 7% zijn gemiddelden over lange perioden, geen jaarlijkse beloftes. Er komen jaren met min tien of min twintig procent, en niemand weet wanneer. Wie dan in paniek verkoopt, maakt van een tijdelijke dip een definitief verlies. Beleggen vraagt dus twee dingen: een horizon van minstens tien jaar, en het temperament om onderweg niet aan de knoppen te zitten. Kun je een van beide niet opbrengen, dan is het hogere eindbedrag in de tabel voor jou een fictief getal.</p> <p>Mijn eigen antwoord is daarom geen óf-óf maar een verdeling. Het geld dat ik binnen enkele jaren nodig heb, plus een buffer van een paar maanden vaste lasten voor noodgevallen, staat op de spaarrekening — daar hoort het veilig en direct beschikbaar te zijn. Alles daarboven, geld dat ik tien jaar of langer kan missen, beleg ik gespreid en saai. Zo hoef ik me bij een beursdaling nooit zorgen te maken over de huur, en hoeft mijn verre-toekomstgeld niet weg te kwijnen onder de inflatie. Sparen en beleggen zijn geen concurrenten; ze doen gewoon elk een andere baan.</p> <p>Waar je geld het hardst groeit, is wiskundig dus duidelijk. Waar het bij jou het beste staat, hangt af van wanneer je het nodig hebt. Wil je je eigen situatie doorrekenen — je eigen maandbedrag, een eigen mix van percentages en looptijden — dan kun je zelf rente op rente berekenen met de gratis calculator van Toolkistje en de scenario's naast elkaar zetten. Reken het een keer uit voor je buffer én voor je lange termijn, en de verdeling maakt zichzelf bijna vanzelf.</p> <p>DEV Community — A space to discuss and keep up software development and manage your software career</p> <p>Built on Forem — the open source software that powers DEV and other inclusive communities.</p> <p>Made with love and Ruby on Rails. DEV Community © 2016 - 2026.</p> <p>We're a place where coders share, stay up-to-date and grow their careers.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://dev.to/toolkistje/sparen-of-beleggen-waar-groeit-je-geld-het-hardst-5572" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9799"> <h2>#9799. Comparing Six AI Video APIs by Cost, Concurrency, and Reliability</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://hackernoon.imgix.net/images/slT3HCgc9CZ4HGESXdHgPgAICaj1-wn83dym.jpeg" alt="Comparing Six AI Video APIs by Cost, Concurrency, and Reliability" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p>Most AI video work still starts in a browser tab: type a prompt, wait, download. That breaks down once a team needs 200 product clips a week, a video step inside an app, or an agent that renders drafts overnight. Video APIs move generation into code. In this article, we: how the requests work, a short working example, what matters once real traffic arrives, six APIs side by side, and the automation layer on top.</p> <p>A video takes anywhere from under a minute to a few minutes to render, so no provider keeps an HTTP connection open until the file is ready. Every major video API follows the same three-part pattern.</p> <p>The names change from provider to provider. fal calls them requests, Replicate calls them predictions, and Runway calls them tasks. The shape stays the same.</p> <p>The example below uses the Higgsfield API and Seedance 2.5. The same submit, poll, and download loop works with any provider. Only the URL, auth header, and field names change.</p> <p>Step 1: Set your credentials. Create an API key in the console and export the key ID and secret.</p> <p>Step 2: Submit the job. The idempotency key lets you resend the same request after a timeout without paying twice.</p> <p>A demo needs one successful call. A production pipeline has to survive timeouts, rate limits, moderation rejections, and bills that grow with every retry. Four areas decide how much work that takes.</p> <p>Every provider caps parallel jobs. Higgsfield allows 20 concurrent requests, fal allows 2 to 40 on self-serve accounts, Runway allows 1 to 20 depending on usage tier, and MiniMax allows 30 in-flight H3 jobs. Put your own job queue in front of the API, such as a database table or a Redis list, so a batch of 500 renders waits its turn instead of failing.</p> <p>Retry network errors and 5xx responses with exponential backoff. Never retry 4xx validation errors, since the same input will fail again. Send an idempotency key with each submission so a resent POST does not start a second paid job. Treat webhooks as at-least-once: Higgsfield, fal, and Replicate can all deliver duplicates, so deduplicate by request ID. Keep a polling fallback in case a webhook never arrives.</p> <p>Failure rules differ more than prices do.</p> <p>Validate inputs before you submit. A broken image URL or an unsupported duration is the cheapest bug to catch.</p> <p>No single model wins every shot. Kling 4.0 handles long takes, Seedance 2.5 handles reference-driven scenes, and MiniMax H3 delivers 2K at a low rate. Calling each vendor directly means separate keys, balances, rate limits, and response formats. Platforms such as Higgsfield, fal, Replicate, and Runway Dev put multiple models behind one key and one balance, so switching models means changing one model ID. The trade-off is dependence on the platform’s pricing and model coverage.</p> <p>Prices are list rates per second of 720p video (768p on MiniMax), checked in late October and early November 2026. Promotions are excluded.</p> <p>50+ video and image models, incl. Kling 4.0, Seedance 2.5, MiniMax H3, Wan 3.0</p> <p>Wan 3.0 from $0.020/s; Kling 4.0 from $0.110/s</p> <p>Gen-4.5 and Aleph, plus Kling 4.0, Seedance 2.5, Gemini Omni</p> <p>Google shut down the three Veo 3.1 preview models in the Gemini API (veo-3.1-generate-preview, veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview, and veo-3.1-lite-generate-preview) on October 22, 2026, and points developers to Gemini Omni Flash instead. The generally available Veo 3.1 models remain on Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.</p> <p>Pick Higgsfield when you want top models plus production tools like consistent characters and camera control behind one key, or fal for a broad open catalog. Replicate fits teams that also deploy custom models. Runway Dev makes sense when Gen-4.5 and Aleph editing sit at the center of the pipeline. The Gemini API suits chat-style edits on Google's own model, and MiniMax wins when 2K output at a low per-second rate matters most.</p> <p>A cron job or a cloud scheduler, such as GitHub Actions, Google Cloud Scheduler, or AWS EventBridge, can read tomorrow's briefs from a sheet or database, submit one job per row, and write the finished URLs back. Pair it with webhooks so the scheduler never sits idle polling.</p> <p>Both connect to any video API through a generic HTTP step, with no custom node required. In n8n, a typical flow runs Schedule Trigger, then HTTP Request to submit, then a Wait node set to resume on a webhook call, then a download and upload to Google Drive or S3. Pass $execution.resumeUrl as the provider's webhook URL so the workflow wakes up when the video is ready. In Make, one scheduled scenario submits jobs through the HTTP module, and a second scenario that starts from a Custom webhook receives results and files them.</p> <p>The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an AI assistant call outside tools directly. Higgsfield's MCP server connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, and other MCP-compatible clients, and gives the agent 30+ image and video models with no API key. A marketer can ask the assistant to make three 9:16 hook variants of a product shot and get the files back without writing code. Agents work best on drafts and one-off requests. Scheduled pipelines still handle volume better.</p> <p>Which AI video API is the cheapest? Per second of output, Wan 3.0 on Higgsfield starts at $0.020, MiniMax H3 runs $0.08 at 768p, and Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash costs about $0.10 at 720p. Count retries too: a cheap model that needs four takes costs more than a pricier one that lands in one.</p> <p>Do I need webhooks, or is polling enough? Polling every 5 to 10 seconds works at low volume. As job counts grow, webhooks cut wasted requests. Keep polling as a fallback either way.</p> <p>How long do providers keep generated videos? Not long. Replicate deletes API outputs after one hour by default, and Higgsfield keeps them at least seven days. Copy each file to your own storage as soon as the job completes.</p> <p>Can I spend web app credits through the API? Usually not. Higgsfield and Runway both bill API usage from a separate prepaid balance, apart from app subscriptions.</p> <p>This article was published under HackerNoon's Business Blogging program.</p> <p>Anyone Can Copy Your Crypto App. Can They Copy Your Business?</p> <p>Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://hackernoon.com/comparing-six-ai-video-apis-by-cost-concurrency-and-reliability?source=rss" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9798"> <h2>#9798. The 12 best recipes to bake in October: It’s peak baking season — here’s what to make.</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/sites/default/files/2026-09/Pumpkin-Milk-Bread_2026_Lifestyle_H_3153.jpg" alt="The 12 best recipes to bake in October: It’s peak baking season — here’s what to make." style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>What do jobs, school, sports practices, and commuting have in common? They all prevent us from baking as much or as often as we’d like. But when we do get the chance, we want a slam-dunk recipe — or 12. Here’s a dozen of the favorite fall recipes we’ll be making this month: from pumpkin cake bars to spooky fudge brownies to a crowd-pleasing vegetarian quiche.</p> <p>It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown! Only this version comes in cake form. The decoration is deceptively easy: Stack two small Bundts, frost the entire thing, and add a chocolate-dipped ice cream cone for the stem.</p> <p>Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Pumpkin Pie Spice</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake, Gluten-Free Pumpkin Cake</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need:  Black Cocoa and Supernatural Plant-Based Food Colors</p> <p>These bite-sized pies are a charming addition to any occasion. The boiled cider and spices in the filling ensure a full depth of apple flavor for maximum fall vibes. If you're tight on time, swap the lattice treatment for a buttery crumb topping instead.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Apple Pie Bars, Tiny Apple Tarts for Two</p> <p>Step aside, soup: Butternut squash truly shines in this autumnal quiche. Caramelized onions finished with balsamic vinegar and fresh baby spinach round out the filling, while our Classic Single Pie Crust recipe ensures a tender, golden crust. Elevate the edges with the pie crust decorating technique of your choice.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Roasted Butternut Squash & Spinach Quiche</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" Pie Pan</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Vegetable Quiche, Delicata Squash Galette with Cheese and Herbs</p> <p>Ready to test the theory that only white flour can make rolls light and fluffy? A bit of bread flour and vital wheat gluten give these whole wheat rolls a lofty rise, while the milk, butter, and honey create a plush crumb that stays soft for days. Add a salted honey butter wash to the tops of a freshly baked batch, and you may not have any leftover.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Super-Soft Whole Wheat Rolls</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Golden Wheat Flour and Bread Flour</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Whole Grain Dinner Rolls, Soft White Dinner Rolls</p> <p>"Tassie" means "small cup" in Scottish, and these dainty pecan pies pack a nutty punch. The cream cheese pastry crust is cut into rounds and placed in a mini muffin pan before the pecan pie filling is spooned into each well. With only 30 minutes of hands-on time, these two dozen tassies come together quickly on a crisp fall afternoon.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Muffin Pan</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Easy Pecan Pie Bars, Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie</p> <p>Need a spooky treat, stat? You can transform a plain batch of brownies into a Halloween-themed dessert in a pinch. A simple piping technique creates a spider web effect and adds a touch of rich tang to chocolatey brownies.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" x 13" Pan</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Fudge Brownies, Chocolate Cheesecake Brownies</p> <p>You’ll notice a lot of similarities between this pumpkin cake and carrot cake: moist, spiced cake, toasted walnuts, and rich cream cheese frosting. These bars are great for delighting a crowd, as this recipe yields three to four dozen bars, depending on how big you slice them. You can easily make them gluten-free, too.</p> <p>Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Maple Syrup</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Pumpkin Spice Latte Bars, Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake</p> <p>'Tis the season for hand pies to be mummified! A shortening-based pie crust helps the lattice strips stay together, while jam or pie filling allows for customizable flavors. Pop on a few sugar eyes, and you'll be sure to have treats instead of tricks.</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Double Pastry Wheel or Pizza Cutter</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Flaky Apple Hand Pies, Autumn Apple Turnovers</p> <p>With a luxuriously creamy maple filling and a buttery pecan crust, this cheesecake balances richness with subtle flavors. Meanwhile, the candied pecan garnish adds visual interest and a complementary crunch. Be sure to leave time for an overnight chill and keep your cheesecake from cracking with these tips. (Find more seasonal maple recipes in our Fall Flavor Edit.)</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Springform Pan</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Caramel Pecan Cheesecake, Maple Cream Pie</p> <p>No need to choose between chocolate or caramel; these cupcakes bring both bold flavors together in a luscious combination. Making caramel from scratch is worth it for the irreplaceable flavor, and those few extra steps are easily done ahead of time. Substitute in Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour to make these cupcakes gluten-free. (Find more seasonal caramel recipes in our Fall Flavor Edit.)</p> <p>Get the recipe: Chocolate Cupcakes with Whipped Caramel Frosting</p> <p>To make this recipe, you’ll need: Muffin Pan and Pastry Brush</p> <p>If you like this recipe, you may also like: Chocolate Cupcakes with Pecan Caramel , S’more Cupcakes</p> <p>This milk bread incorporates all the flavor and color of pumpkin, while still keeping an airy texture. You can shape the dough into pull-apart rolls or a loaf, and topping with a milk wash and pumpkin seeds adds a nutty crunch. Wrap it Measuring the Impact of Expo Router Deep Links</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fxrxvrrwrlpyszlrwxgkk.supabase.co%2Fstorage%2Fv1%2Fobject%2Fpublic%2Fproject-images%2Fblog%2Fexpo-router-deep-links-measuring-before-optimising.jpg" alt="Measuring the Impact of Expo Router Deep Links" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at amitchakraborty.dev</p> <p>Say you are a mobile app developer working on a React Native project using Expo Router. You've heard about the benefits of deep links, but you're not sure if implementing them will have a significant impact on your app's performance. You've tried to measure the effect of deep links on your app's routing, but you're not sure what metrics to track or how to instrument your app to get meaningful data.</p> <p>You were trying to optimize your app's routing to improve user experience, but you're not sure if the effort will be worth it. You've seen a symptom - a noticeable delay when navigating between screens - but you don't know if it's related to deep links or something else. The delay is costing you users, who are abandoning your app due to frustration with its performance.</p> <p>Expo Router deep links can improve app performance by allowing the app to navigate directly to a specific screen, rather than loading the entire app and then navigating to the desired screen. However, implementing deep links requires changes to your app's routing configuration, which can be complex and time-consuming. To determine whether the effort is worth it, you need to measure the impact of deep links on your app's performance.</p> <p>One key metric to track is the time it takes for the app to navigate between screens. This can be measured using the navigation module in Expo Router, which provides a navigate function that returns a promise that resolves when the navigation is complete. You can use this promise to measure the time it takes for the navigation to complete, and compare it to the time it takes without deep links.</p> <p>To measure the impact of Expo Router deep links on your app's performance, follow these steps:</p> <p>Implementing Expo Router deep links can require significant changes to your app's routing configuration, which can be time-consuming and may require additional testing. However, if your app has a complex routing hierarchy or requires frequent navigation between screens, the benefits of deep links may outweigh the costs.</p> <p>In general, deep links are most beneficial for apps that:</p> <p>On the other hand, deep links may not be necessary for apps that:</p> <p>When interviewing a candidate for a React Native developer position, you may ask a question like: "How would you measure the impact of Expo Router deep links on app performance?" A weak answer might focus on the benefits of deep links without discussing how to measure their impact. A strong answer would describe the instrumentation technique outlined above, including how to measure navigation time and compare it to the navigation time with deep links. The candidate should also be able to discuss the trade-offs between implementing deep links and other optimization techniques, and evaluate the impact of deep links on user engagement metrics. A follow-up question might ask the candidate to describe a scenario in which deep links would not be necessary, and how they would determine whether the benefits of deep links outweigh the costs.</p> <p>Amit Chakraborty is a founding engineer and senior architect — React Native, AI/RAG systems and production architecture. The DevOps bootcamp · 4. Git as an operations tool</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=1200,height=627,fit=cover,gravity=auto,format=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fxrxvrrwrlpyszlrwxgkk.supabase.co%2Fstorage%2Fv1%2Fobject%2Fpublic%2Fproject-images%2Fblog%2Fdevops-bootcamp-4-git-as-an-operations-tool.jpg" alt="The DevOps bootcamp · 4. Git as an operations tool" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Posted on Nov 13 • Originally published at amitchakraborty.dev</p> <p>The DevOps bootcamp · Chapter 4 of 14 · DevOps · new chapter every Thursday morning</p> <p>By the end of this chapter: Use branches, tags and history the way a delivery pipeline reads them.</p> <p>You are a junior engineer on your first backend project, and you need to test a branch on the team's shared staging server. You SSH into the server, pull your code, and run the start command. However, the terminal returns an error message: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::8080. This error indicates that another process is already using port 8080, which is the port your application is trying to use.</p> <p>You try changing the port, but the proxy routing traffic to your application expects it to be running on port 8080. You assume the previous version of the application is still running, but you do not know how to find it. You try running your new application as the superuser to force it through, and it starts, but immediately crashes with Permission denied: /var/log/staging-api/error.log. This error message suggests that your application does not have the necessary permissions to write to the log file.</p> <p>You have wasted an hour trying to troubleshoot the issue, and you are still no closer to testing your branch. You need to understand how to manage different versions of your application, how to find and stop running processes, and how to handle permissions issues.</p> <p>To follow along with this chapter, you need to have Git installed on your machine, and you should have a basic understanding of Linux commands, such as navigating the file system and running processes. You should also have a Git repository set up for your project. You can verify that Git is installed by running the command git --version in your terminal. The output should display the version of Git installed on your machine, such as git version 2.37.1.</p> <p>In Git, a branch is a separate line of development in your repository. You can think of it as a separate copy of your codebase that you can work on independently of the main codebase. When you create a new branch, Git creates a new pointer to the current commit, and any changes you make will be committed to that branch.</p> <p>To create a new branch, you can use the command git branch <branch-name>. For example, to create a new branch called feature/new-feature, you would run the command git branch feature/new-feature. You can then switch to that branch using the command git checkout feature/new-feature.</p> <p>Git tags are used to mark specific points in your repository's history. They are often used to mark releases or milestones. To create a new tag, you can use the command git tag <tag-name>. For example, to create a new tag called v1.0, you would run the command git tag v1.0.</p> <p>Git history refers to the record of all changes made to your repository over time. You can view the history of your repository using the command git log. This will display a list of all commits made to your repository, including the commit message, author, and date.</p> <p>To solve the problem of testing a branch on the shared staging server, you can follow these steps:</p> <p>Here are some common issues you may encounter when working with Git branches and tags:</p> <p>Using Git branches and tags can have some costs, such as:</p> <p>However, the benefits of using Git branches and tags, such as being able to work on multiple features independently and marking specific points in your repository's history, outweigh the costs.</p> <p>In an interview, you may be asked questions such as:</p> <p>Note: These tasks are designed to be completed in a real-world scenario, and may require additional setup and configuration depending on your specific environment.</p> <p>Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.</p> <p>Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened: tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.</p> <p>Chapter 4 of 14. New chapter every Thursday morning. Our top-ranked cookie recipes: Eight cookies that have stood the test of time.</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/sites/default/files/2026-04/Classic-Chocolate-Chip-Cookie-10.jpg" alt="Our top-ranked cookie recipes: Eight cookies that have stood the test of time." style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Every time you, a reader, posts a comment, it gives me a chance to reflect on the recipe. When the comment is positive, I'm proud and happy; my kid just scored the winning goal!</p> <p>When a recipe gets a not-so-good comment, I'm bummed. Bad report card. Thankfully, most of our reviewed recipes get four or five stars. And some get LOTS of four- and five-star reviews. These are our straight-A students; our all-stars.
