People With Depression May Be Missing Something Their Brains Normally Produce (M)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/brain-4-4.jpg" alt="People With Depression May Be Missing Something Their Brains Normally Produce (M)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>A change deep inside the brain could help explain why depression makes negative experiences so difficult to escape.</p> <p>A change deep inside the brain could help explain why depression makes negative experiences so difficult to escape.</p> <p>• Read members-only articles • Adverts removed • Cancel at any time • 14 day money-back guarantee for new members</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.spring.org.uk/2026/10/depression-neurogenesis.php" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9667"> <h2>#9667. Three Qualities That Can Make You an Inspiring Leader</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/three_things_that_make_you_an_inspiring_leader_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.webp" alt="Three Qualities That Can Make You an Inspiring Leader" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>Imagine you’re on a plane and suddenly hear an explosion. The whole plane rattles, and you see the left engine is on fire. After another loud noise, you realize there’s a hole in the side of the aircraft. As air rushes out, the plane is rapidly descending—over 20,000 feet in less than five minutes.</p> <p>If you faced what passengers of Southwest Airlines 1380 experienced, you would probably do what they did: frantically write goodbye messages to your family and loved ones, thinking that these are your last moments on Earth.</p> <p>But on that flight, the pilot, Captain Tammie Jo Shults, came on the intercom and said 10 simple words: “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.”</p> <p>The passengers would later talk about how those 10 words were transformative, turning their panic into possibility. By sharing those 10 words, Captain Shults was helping her passengers make sense of their experience and reframe the dramatic descent, from “plummeting to Earth” to a planned and orchestrated path to safety.</p> <p>As Captain Shults expertly landed the plane, she calmly and peacefully talked to air traffic control. After landing, she got up and went row by row, looking every passenger in the eye to make sure they were OK. People talked afterward about her words, her stature, and her empathy as she walked down that aisle.</p> <p>Contrast Captain Shults’s experience with another captain who also dealt with a massive hole in his vessel, Francesco Schettino, captain of the Costa Concordia. Headed out on a seven-day cruise in the Mediterranean, the ship got too close to shore. It’s debatable why that happened: Captain Schettino claims he was saluting mariners on the shore; prosecutors claim he was trying to impress his mistress who was on board. But what isn’t in dispute is what happened next: The rocks tore a 115-foot hole in the side of the ship, which caused it to eventually capsize.</p> <p>Before calling the Coast Guard, Captain Schettino spent time getting his story straight. The crash had caused an electrical blackout, but he was going to try to say that the blackout caused the crash. He tried to pin the responsibility on the helmsman. It took him almost an hour after the crash to sound the evacuation siren.</p> <p>While people were frantically trying to find safety, Captain Schettino was nowhere to be found. Finally, the Coast Guard discovered him in a lifeboat—though Captain Schettino claimed that he “accidentally” fell into the lifeboat. But he also somehow fell out of his captain’s uniform. He was sitting in a lifeboat watching his boat sinking, hiding in civilian clothing. You can hear the outrage in the Coast Guard’s voice when he says in an audio recording, “I’m gonna make you pay for this.” And Captain Schettino did pay. He was sentenced to 12 years in prison for manslaughter and abandoning ship.</p> <p>These two people faced very similar situations. They were both captains, dealing with holes in the side of their vessels, but how they responded to their crises was completely different. Captain Shults helped people make sense of their experience. She was courageous, competent, and calm in landing the plane, and she compassionately connected to each of her passengers. In contrast, Captain Schettino caused the accident, refused to take any responsibility, and did not take any action to help his passengers save their lives. As a result of his selfish negligence, 32 people died, and numerous people were injured.</p> <p>Why do some leaders create feelings of inspiration that percolate a wellspring of hope and possibility in others, while other leaders create seething cauldrons of infuriation and resentment? I’ve asked this question to tens of thousands of people across the globe, and here is what I learned about what makes a leader inspiring.</p> <p>My first big idea is that “inspiring” and “infuriating” leaders exist on an enduring continuum that is made up of three universal factors:</p> <p>We can inspire people in how we communicate, how we present ourselves, and how we interact with others—through our words, our actions, and our interactions.</p> <p>My second big idea is that these are the three factors of inspiring leadership because each one fulfills a fundamental human need. Being visionary fulfills the fundamental need for meaning and understanding. That’s what Captain Shults provided when she said, “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.” She helped people make sense of their experience.</p> <p>Being an exemplar fulfills the fundamental need for protection and passion. Captain Shults courageously protected her passengers with her calm and competence.</p> <p>And being a mentor fulfills the fundamental human need for belonging and status. That’s what Captain Shults offered as she walked down the aisle: She made her passengers feel recognized and seen.</p> <p>By surveying tens of thousands of people across the globe, I have found these three dimensions to be universal. There is not a single inspiring characteristic that is mentioned in one country that’s not mentioned in the dozens of countries in the world where I have collected data.</p> <p>Effective visionaries not only offer a clear perspective on the world, but they also make their vision easy to follow and understand, and so engaging that it captures our attention.</p> <p>The easiest way to make something easy is to make it simple. I call this the Inception Rule, after the movie Inception, where Leonardo DiCaprio tries to plant an idea in someone’s head during a dream. He discovers it’s not about how deep you go; it’s about how simple the idea is. As a leader, you want to constantly be thinking how to reduce your ideas to their simple core.</p> <p>Another way that we can make things easy to understand is to repeat them, the way a chorus repeats in a song. The more people hear it, the more they will remember it.</p> <p>Let’s consider Zoom’s vision: Delivering Happiness. It’s simple, and bubbly. But that vision is also deeply practical—it helped Zoom’s employees efficiently make high-stakes decisions during the chaos of the COVID-19 pandemic. As millions of people began using the product for the first time, Zoom needed to decide on its product’s baseline level of functionality. Too many features would overwhelm people, but too few features would stymie people. They needed the Goldilocks baseline of features to deliver happiness.</p> <p>Similarly, delivering happiness led Zoom to invest heavily in customer service. Most of us know how much an hour-long wait for customer service can destroy happiness. So, Zoom hired many agents so wait times would be as short as possible.</p> <p>To make our visions more engaging, we can use visual language. Andrew Carton, an associate professor of management at Wharton, did a study where people were told that a company’s mission was to either “make our customers satisfied” or “make our customers smile.” Then, he had people create a product. When they were working under the more visual vision (“smile”), they created more engaging products.</p> <p>How to become more visionary: We can inspire people to be more visionary by having them reflect on their values. In one of my studies, we worked with a Swiss employment agency. When people came in to register for benefits, half of them were asked to reflect on their values, why those values mattered to them, and how they demonstrated them. For example, my own values include generosity, courage, and kaizen (a Japanese word for continued improvement).</p> <p>Two months later, the people who had reflected on their values were twice as likely to have a job. The effects were so profound that the employment agency asked us to end our study and give everyone the reflection activity.</p> <p>To be a great exemplar, the first thing you want to do is to consistently embody your vision; don’t be a hypocrite. As former CEO of PepsiCo Indra Nooyi once noted, “Don’t ask someone to do something that you wouldn’t do [yourself].”</p> <p>Inspiring exemplars are calm and courageous protectors, like Captain Shults. And they show passion. When you ask someone to talk about a passion of theirs, their eyes light up, they smile a big beaming smile, they speak quickly and dramatically use their hands, and they lean in as if telling you a secret. When we are passionate about something, it’s revealed in our eyes, our mouth, our voice, and our bodies. And when you listen to someone’s passion, you smile, your eyes light up, and you feel the energy inside of you.</p> <p>Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series</p> <p>In my research on Dragon’s Den, which is a variant of Shark Tank, when entrepreneurs expressed more passion—in their eyes, their voice, their hands—they were dramatically more likely to receive funding. You can’t inspire others if you aren’t inspired.</p> <p>How to become a better exemplar: Think about the moments in your life when you felt the most powerful and in control, your best self. Hundreds of studies around the world have used this technique that my colleagues Deb Gruenfeld, Joe Magee, and I created. We’ve even found that people are more likely to be selected for jobs if they’ve engaged in this reflection.</p> <p>Consider this proverb by Confucius: “Tell me and I will forget, show me and I may remember, involve me and I will understand.” When you involve people, they feel seen and heard and they feel like people, not objects.</p> <p>Inspiring leaders empower others everywhere across the globe. Even in cultures that are less individualistic than the United States—like Thailand or Saudi Arabia—there’s nothing more infuriating than when a boss micromanages you, rather than involves you or trusts you.</p> <p>Inspiring leaders also elevate others. They share credit rather than steal credit, which is one of the most infuriating things that can happen at work. Finally, inspiring leaders empathize with others. They do what Captain Shults did, in making sure each of her passengers were OK, versus only thinking about themselves, like Captain Schettino.</p> <p>How to become a better mentor: Reflect on the perspectives of others. My colleagues and I did a study with medical students who were tasked with diagnosing what was wrong with patients. Before meeting their patients, half the students were told to take the perspectives of their patients and to think about a recent time when they had engaged in perspective taking. Ultimately, the patients were more satisfied, trusting, and likely to follow the advice of the doctor who had been reminded to engage in perspective taking.</p> <p>My third big idea is that inspiring leaders aren’t just born; they’re also made. Because there is a universal set of inspiring attributes and behaviors, they can be practiced, nurtured, and developed.</p> <p>My fourth big idea is that when you’re a leader, you don’t have the option of not having an impact. Your behavior is going to inspire or infuriate. I call this the “leader amplification effect.” Everything you say and do as a leader gets amplified. Your criticisms become humiliating criticisms, but your compliments become glorious praise.</p> <p>My fifth big idea is that you can REIP what you sow. This phrase, drawn from the Bible, suggests that if we put inspiring energy out in the world, we receive inspiring energy in return. But my REIP is a homonym of reap, and it stands for reflect, emulate, intend, and practice:</p> <p>My final big idea is that inspiring leaders think like architects. Like an architect who designs buildings to produce particular reactions and interactions, leaders design policies and practices that lead people down the inspiring path, even when they’re not present. So instead of just changing individual behavior, you can think about: How can you change a broader dynamic?</p> <p>Thinking like an architect moves you from viewing a situation as a person problem—What’s wrong with this employee?—to start to think about what’s wrong in their environment, and how you can redesign that environment to help the employee be the best version of themselves.</p> <p>Here’s one practice that Joseph Stagliano, president of NBT Bank, designed to inspire those around him. Although he has over 1,200 employees, he sends a birthday greeting to every single person. That sounds impossible, but he does it in 10 to 15 minutes over coffee every day.</p> <p>The message is simple yet personalized. He showed me an example that said, “Hey Monica [pseudonym], Happy birthday! I hope you had a great weekend? How did track and bowling go?” Although his message was short, Monica’s response was extensive, overflowing with information and enthusiasm.</p> <p>I shared that idea with the CEO of another company, and then a month later, he told me he started doing something similar. Every morning over coffee, he reached out to one person in his organization, and he expressed either gratitude or praise. He said he did this to put a skip in their step, but they ended up sending him such glowing replies that it put a skip in his step. The CEO reaped the inspiring energy he sowed. You can, too.</p> <p>This essay is based on a talk that is part of the Positive Links Speaker Series by the University of Michigan’s Center for Positive Organizations. The Center is dedicated to building a better world by pioneering the science of thriving organizations.</p> <p>Adam Galinsky is a professor at the Columbia Business School. He is author or co-author of more than 200 scientific articles, the bestselling book INSPIRE: The Universal Path for Leading Yourself and Others (HarperCollins, 2025), the bestselling book Friend & Foe (Penguin Random House, 2015), and a popular TED talk, How to Speak Up for Yourself, with over 7.8 million views.</p> <p>Generous parental leave policies improve health for moms and babies, family finances, and equality at work and at home.</p> <p>Try these Greater Good in Action practices to build appreciation, trust, and kindness in your workplace.</p> <p>Hunter‑gatherer societies are often put on a pedestal for being truly egalitarian—but the reality is more complicated.</p> <p>How happy are you when you’re on the clock?</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/three_qualities_that_can_make_you_an_inspiring_leader" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9666"> <h2>#9666. Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Easy-Vegetarian-Eggplant-Bolognese-9.jpg" alt="Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!</p> <p>Even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!</p> <p>Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.</p> <p>Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!</p> <p>This 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).</p> <p>Build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.</p> <p>Once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!</p> <p>When it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.</p> <p>We think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!</p> <p>It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>This recipe is perfect. I did add the ground beef into the recipe as noted, so had to increase the salt, red pepper flakes, and Italian seasoning. Was so delicious!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Meg! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo</p> <p>So glad you enjoyed it, Don! Thanks so much for sharing!</p> <p>I love the idea of turning eggplant into a hearty bolognese, especially when it can all be made in one pot. Eggplant can soak up so much flavor, so it seems like a really good fit for a rich tomato-based sauce. I also appreciate recipes like this that make a meat-free meal feel filling rather than like a compromise. Definitely adding this one to my list to try.</p> <p>THIS WAS SO EASY AND SO RICH! I MADE CASHEW MILK AND USED CABERNET TO DREDGE UP THE PIECES. I DON’T USUALLY MAKE MY OWN SAUCES BUT THIS WAS A REAL WINNER WITH GREAT BODY AND RICHNESS. JUST LOVED AND WILL BE A STAPLE..</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo</p> <p>Made this for the first time and love it! Thank you for making simple vegan recipes!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Christine! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo</p> <p>I made this. I substituted the tomato ingredients with my first every tomato sauce made with fresh tomatoes from my garden. I also used cashew cream and added a pepper from the garden. Delicious. What a great recipe for eggplant.</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Heidi! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo</p> <p>This was absolutely delicious. However I did substitute chopped zucchini for the carrots. It was very flavorful and quite satisfying. I’m going to try putting it on a plain pizza crust next and sprinkle it with cheese for a new type of pizza bolognese. Thank you so much for this recipe.</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Makenzie! Thanks so much for the lovely review. Pizza Bolognese sounds delicious!</p> <p>Ooh, I just drooled a little. I’ll be adding this to my “must try soon” list!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2023/09/PSYCH_1000x1000.png" alt="Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”</p> <p>The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.</p> <p>Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.</p> <p>The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.</p> <p>This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.</p> <p>This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.</p> <p>This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor</p> <p>Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832</p> <p>Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://www.psychiatryadvisor.com/home/topics/addiction/opioid-related-disorder/fentanyl-challenges-current-methadone-induction-protocols/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9664"> <h2>#9664. Easy Seasoned Pretzels</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><h2><a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/moms-seasoned-pretzels/">Easy Seasoned Pretzels</a></h2> <div style="text-align: center;"><img alt="seasoned pretzel pieces in a bowl." class="attachment-post-thumbnail size-post-thumbnail wp-image-159134 wp-post-image" height="1800" src="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/12/easy-seasoned-hard-pretzels.jpg" width="1200" /></div> <p>I've served these seasoned pretzels on repeat for over a decade because they're VERY easy and VERY crowd pleasing. Deliciously savory and crunchy—I say with confidence that you will not be able to stop snacking on these. Just read some of the reviews!</p> <p>The post <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/moms-seasoned-pretzels/">Easy Seasoned Pretzels</a> appeared first on <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com">Sally's Baking</a>.</p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/moms-seasoned-pretzels/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9663"> <h2>#9663. 1-Bowl Honey Almond Snack Cake (Gluten-Free)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Gluten-Free-Honey-Cake-15-683x1024.jpg" alt="1-Bowl Honey Almond Snack Cake (Gluten-Free)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Honey almond snack cake!? You know you want to jump in on the fun! This GORGEOUS loaf is perfectly moist with a lightly floral flavor and beautiful sponge texture. Bonus? It’s made without gluten or dairy, but no one will know.</p> <p>It’s the perfect cake for afternoon tea, brunch gatherings, and beyond! Just 10 ingredients, 1 bowl, and simple methods (no mixer) required. Let’s bake!</p> <p>This light, fluffy gluten-free honey almond cake is made with 10 simple ingredients:</p> <p>After mixing together your wet ingredients, then adding your dry ingredients, it’s time to pour the batter into a parchment-lined loaf pan. The parchment paper will prevent sticking and make it super easy to remove the cake from the pan.</p> <p>We also think this cake would work beautifully in an 8-inch round cake pan, but it will bake much faster!</p> <p>Top with sliced almonds before baking, then pop that beauty in the oven! After baking and letting the cake cool slightly, we love to add an extra drizzle of honey. Deliciousness awaits, friends!</p> <p>We hope you LOVE this honey almond cake! It’s:FluffyFloralSpongySubtly sweetPerfectly moist& SO delicious!</p> <p>Grab a slice of cake, pour yourself a mug of coffee or tea, kick back, and get your snack on! It would also pair well with Earl Grey Tea, our Lemon Ginger Jasmine Iced Tea, or a Cinnamon Vanilla Dandelion Tea Latte.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>Can this be made without honey? If so, what would be the substitute?</p> <p>Hi Jessica, perhaps agave or maple syrup, but we haven’t tested with those alternatives. The flavor will vary, especially if using maple. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>wow – I absolutely loved this! Incredible flavor and very tender crumb… I can’t believe this combo of pantry ingredients could produce such a fantastic GF cake. And full disclosure – I was kind of winging it with what I had, so I made a version of GF flour with potato starch, white rice flour, sourgum flour and oat flour, and I only had whole almonds so I chopped them roughly for the top. I baked it in my air fryer – a total experiment, and I had to cover it with foil after 10 minutes (did it in an 8×8 pan) – and while it didn’t come out perfectly (it cooked a little unevenly), it was utterly delicious! So moist, with the browned sides and beautifully browned almonds (a benefit of the air fryer, maybe). All to say – this recipe is very adaptable and honestly so so scrumptious. I just had to tell you!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Ann! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo</p> <p>Could I use almond meal instead of almond flour? Or would the change in texture be too drastic?</p> <p>Hey Serena! We think it would work, but the flavor and texture might change a bit! Let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Honey almond snack cake looks like the perfect simple bake. Appreciate how approachable the steps stay while still feeling special — trying a small cake for weekend coffee.</p> <p>I made this as written (but with butter) and it is delightful! I love everything about it! Thanks for another great recipe!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Lisa! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo</p> <p>Made this and loooove it! Came out really fluffy and delicious. Only modification is brand – I used Earth balance plant butter and Silk protein vegan vanilla yogurt. I also baked slightly longer as the core was still really wet at 45 minutes. Ended up being closer to 55-57mins in my oven. Great recipe, thanks!</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Teya! Thanks so much for sharing. xo</p> <p>I made this and it came out delicious. I was wondering if I could 1/2 cup of applesauce for added moisture?</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it! Applesauce might make it a bit too dense, but let us know if you do any experimenting!</p> <p>I followed the recipe and I added 1/2 cup unsweetened applesauce. It added a nice flavor (apples go well with honey) and it made it moist. It was a tiny bit more dense, but it helped to maintain the texture throughout the week.</p> <p>We’re so glad you enjoyed it with the applesauce, Susan! Thanks so much for sharing. xo</p> <p>I made this today with flax egg and it came out beautifully.</p> <p>Some specifics: My flax egg was made with aquafaba instead of water (I had some handy from a fresh pot of chickpeas). My flour was a GF flour from my local grocery store’s private label. I baked it in an 8″ round glass cake pan in my toaster oven. My crumb was tender but a little more dense than yours (and darker due to the flax and my blend of flour).</p> <p>We’re so glad the flax egg worked, Sara! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo</p> <p>Hi! Where do you manage to find Miyoko’s vegan butter? We live in Florida and sadly I haven’t been able to find it at our Whole Foods for almost a year already!! So sad as it has no replacement! Also – I love honey in cakes but stopped using it as heated honey is unhealthy. Would maple work here if I can get the butter?</p> <p>Hey there! Sprouts usually has Miyoko’s if Whole Food’s doesn’t. You could also use another vegan butter here. We have learned that heated honey isn’t necessarily unhealthy, heating it just get’s rid of some of the benefits of raw honey. It’s still safe to bake with! We’re not sure if maple syrup would work, but let us know if you try it!</p> <p>Sounds like another great recipe! Do you think I make it in muffin tins instead? How long would the bake time be then? Thank you! /Mattis</p> <p>Hey Mattis! We haven’t tried the recipe as muffins, but we think it would definitely work! We would suggest starting with a 23 minute bake time and then checking them every 3-5 minutes after until done! Let us know if you try it.</p> <p>This recipe is perfect for Rosh Hashanah shana! I can’t wait to make it for the high holidays. Do you think that I could add chunks of apple or decorate it with sliced apples on top?</p> <p>We’re so glad, Caryn! We’re not sure exactly how the cake would react to the apple, but our suggestion would be if you do add chunks to the cake to coat them in a little flour first to make sure they don’t sink to the bottom! Then you can fold the flour coated apples into the cake right before you add the batter to the pan. They might work on top of the cake, but we would suggest watching it while it bakes to make sure they don’t burn! Let us know if you try it either way!</p> <p>I think I’m going to try subbing sourdough starter for yogurt–I’ll report back with results!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.Email *NameSubmit</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE! Spiced Cranberry Cherry Cobbler</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><h2><a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/cranberry-cherry-cobbler/">Spiced Cranberry Cherry Cobbler</a></h2> <div style="text-align: center;"><img alt="spiced cranberry cherry cobbler in a baking dish topped with vanilla ice cream." class="attachment-post-thumbnail size-post-thumbnail wp-image-168769 wp-post-image" height="1800" src="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/spiced-cherry-cranberry-cobbler.jpg" width="1200" /></div> <p>This spiced cranberry cherry cobbler combines sweet cherries and tart cranberries with a warmly spiced buttery biscuit topping. Orange zest, cinnamon, and nutmeg add cozy flavor, while a little brown sugar gives the tender biscuits a hint of sweetness. The fruit filling thickens as it bakes, bubbling up around the golden fluffy topping. Serve it warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream for a comforting dessert that's especially welcome during the fall and winter months.</p> <p>The post <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/cranberry-cherry-cobbler/">Spiced Cranberry Cherry Cobbler</a> appeared first on <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com">Sally's Baking</a>.</p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/cranberry-cherry-cobbler/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9661"> <h2>#9661. Chocolate Caramel Pecan Tart</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p><h2><a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/chocolate-caramel-pecan-tart/">Chocolate Caramel Pecan Tart</a></h2> <div style="text-align: center;"><img alt="chocolate caramel pecan tart slices." class="attachment-post-thumbnail size-post-thumbnail wp-image-168846 wp-post-image" height="1800" src="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/dark-chocolate-caramel-pecan-tart.jpg" width="1200" /></div> <p>This chocolate caramel pecan tart combines a buttery chocolate pastry crust with a rich, chewy chocolate caramel filling and plenty of toasted pecans. Every slice delivers the perfect mix of chocolate, caramel, and nutty crunch, and a sprinkle of flaky sea salt on top brings it all together. Cook the filling on the stovetop, then let the refrigerator do the rest. This is a wonderful make-ahead dessert!</p> <p>The post <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/chocolate-caramel-pecan-tart/">Chocolate Caramel Pecan Tart</a> appeared first on <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com">Sally's Baking</a>.</p></p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://sallysbakingaddiction.com/chocolate-caramel-pecan-tart/" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9660"> <h2>#9660. Four Ways to Help Newcomers Feel Like They Belong</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://ggsc.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/assets/images/four_ways_to_welcome_people_to_your_community_-_abcdef_-_0a21b39134b316e51cdc0dd96c5e6bca3c0093e9-fb_-_abcdef_-_94b15742ccdfc3b16fb1fe35872167fe8d42c35d.webp" alt="Four Ways to Help Newcomers Feel Like They Belong" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.</p> <p>Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education</p> <p>Liz Cahill was born and raised in Philadelphia. Her whole family is from Philadelphia, going back generations. One day, she was offered an internship in the Bay Area and decided to make the leap, despite not knowing anything about it or anyone there.</p> <p>“I said goodbye to everything I knew and loved in Philadelphia and came to the Bay. Not knowing a soul.”</p> <p>When she arrived, it hit her. “I was like, wow, I’m in a place that like, literally nobody knows me. So if I am dead in a ditch, like nobody will figure it out for a long time.”</p> <p>This could have been a story of loneliness and disconnection, but it wasn’t, because someone took her under their wings—actually two strangers, her roommates Lauren and Deirdre. “They took me in and welcomed me and brought me into their whole social world, which showed me so much love.”</p> <p>This isn’t the experience for most people. Darilys Matos Acevedo grew up in Puerto Rico. “In Puerto Rico, a stranger talks to you all the time. If you went down the street and you talked to somebody, if you made eye contact . . . you had to smile at them or you said good morning or good afternoon.”</p> <p>Then she moved to Boston for graduate school. “I had never even visited the place. I knew nobody here.” And where she got smiles and small talk in Puerto Rico, in Boston she “got glares.” “And I’m like, oh, OK. You don’t do any of that here.” It was painful and created a large void in her life.</p> <p>As Darilys talked to other Latinos in Boston, she assumed “I’m the only one who feels this way, but I wasn’t. There was like a whole group of people that felt like that.”</p> <p>Their stories are different, but they reveal the same truth.</p> <p>Moving doesn’t simply change where we live. It interrupts the invisible web of relationships that makes everyday life feel familiar, that makes us feel like we belong. And the majority of the 13 million American adults who move each year experience this.</p> <p>At the US Chamber of Connection, our recent study on social connection in America explored the impact of life transitions on social connection. It found that 40% of people navigating a relocation struggle with social connection, and they report 35% more barriers to connection compared to everyone else. Two of the most common barriers are not knowing where to start and not wanting to go out alone.</p> <p>The impact is lasting, as someone shared with us. “Two years ago, I was going on a vacation, and I could not find ONE neighbor to water my plants while I was away. I had lived in this building on and off for over 15 years. I was mortified. How could it be that I had nobody in my building to help with such a small task?”</p> <p>Moving ranks among the most stressful life events a person can experience, on par with divorce and job loss. But the stress isn’t just logistical; it’s psychological. Moving severs the informal ties and daily routines that quietly anchor our sense of who we are and where we belong. The result is a predictable but rarely named experience: not just loneliness, but identity dislocation. The question isn’t only “who do I know here?” but “who am I here?”</p> <p>This month, we're teaming up with the US Chamber of Connection for Welcome Week. Together, we're mobilizing communities, neighborhoods, and organizations nationwide to do one simple thing this September: open the door to a new friend. Make a pledge to invite someone in and help us reach our goal to make 100,000 people feel welcomed!</p> <p>To understand the scale of that loss, consider what a typical adult social network requires to build: roughly 200 hours to develop a close friend, 90 hours for a friend, and five hours of repeated interaction for each of the weak ties (neighbors, familiar faces, community contacts) that make daily life feel anchored. A typical adult carries around 1,300 hours of accumulated relationship time. When you move, you leave all of it behind and start from zero.</p> <p>This is also, paradoxically, what makes the first year after a move one of the most powerful windows for connection. Disruption breaks old habits and makes people unusually open to forming new ones, a phenomenon researchers call the habit discontinuity effect. People who have just moved are more likely to join things, try things, and reach out than they were six months earlier at home.</p> <p>What closes that window isn’t lack of desire. Research by Nicholas Epley at the University of Chicago finds that people systematically underestimate how much strangers want to connect and overestimate how awkward the attempt will be. Both the newcomer and the potential neighbor hold back, each assuming the other isn’t interested. Both tend to be wrong.</p> <p>And the effects of getting it right last longer than most people expect. Vanessa Elias, the founder of Block Party USA, shared with us the story of a neighbor who brought her family a pie when she moved in as a six year old. She remembers her name, Mrs. Fisher, decades later.</p> <p>What would happen if welcoming became a civic practice instead of an individual virtue? This year, the US Chamber of Connection recruited over 250 people across 25 states to run creative experiments that aimed to help others feel more welcome in their neighborhoods. They were trained on the science of connection and worked together across the country to support each other. We call them the Welcome Committee.</p> <p>For many of the volunteers, they signed up because they had an experience like Liz. One shared that “when we arrived to our new town we felt welcomed, surprised, and alive through these touches, and wanted to build more.” Or as another volunteer explained, “people are still welcoming me and I still feel at home here. So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I wanna create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”</p> <p>For others, it came from an experience more akin to Darilys’s. “I would have loved to find this kind of thing when I moved,” shared one early volunteer. “I’ve been in my neighborhood and city since 2019 and have yet to make close friends in the neighborhood or city where I live. It feels scary and uncomfortable to get out there. But I’m realizing the huge impact of not having close friends. I’m ready to make the effort. Because if I’m feeling this way, I can’t be the only one.”</p> <p>They each began by inviting a neighbor for a conversation. They shared their stories of their neighborhoods growing up. Dreamed about the ideal neighborhood together. Explored the Six Points of Connection, a clear and actionable checklist for individuals and leaders to define and strengthen social bonds. And then they explored how they might together make the neighborhood more connected.</p> <p>They ran some creative experiments. Lindsay turned their suburban garage door into a community message board. Kaitlin created a traveling tin of homemade baked goods that moves neighbor to neighbor down the street, each recipient required to bake something and pass it on to someone new. Sarah hosted a gathering for other people named Sara(h) in her town. Courtney started flyering the neighborhood to organize a dog gathering in someone’s backyard. Nithya left a flower and a handwritten note for each of the five nearest neighbors inviting them to coffee.</p> <p>Many of the volunteers nostalgically tried things they remembered from their childhood or had seen in a movie. Kate moved an iron chair and table to her front step and started having her morning coffee there facing the street. Jon made lemonade with his kids and set out donuts for anyone walking by. Chet started introducing himself on his daily dog walks. Anne organized a multi-household yard sale across eight houses. And many of them hosted potlucks and block parties.</p> <p>They all expressed knowing “how meaningful it can be to walk into a new space and find someone who is genuinely glad you are there.” And they wanted to make people feel that way.</p> <p>As the volunteers conducted their experiments, they began to share their findings. They mirrored much of what we have learned from social scientists over the last 50 years. Four themes emerged that help to inform how we can all do more to help new residents, and any neighbor, feel more welcomed.</p> <p>1. The first step is the most important. Stop playing “invite chicken.” Many of our volunteers shared a version of the same experience: sitting at home hoping someone would call and invite them to hang out, attend an event, or even just watch Netflix together. They assumed that the people they wanted to call were probably busy or uninterested. Those people were likely sitting at home thinking the same thing. Nobody called. Everyone stayed alone.</p> <p>Call it invite chicken: a standoff where everyone loses despite everyone wanting the same thing. The barrier isn’t reality; it’s anticipation. Someone just has to go first.</p> <p>And sometimes, when we do break the game of chicken, we don’t get the response we wanted. When Hazel hosted her first neighborhood coffee gathering, one neighbor texted that he was too nervous to come. She didn’t give up. She texted back encouraging him. He came. At one of Elizabeth’s gatherings in San Diego, a man had been dragged along by his wife, who promised they’d stay just five minutes. He was the last to leave.</p> <p>We are poor forecasters of our own social experiences. People overweight the discomfort of initiation and underweight the pleasure of connection. The host who sends the follow-up text, the wife who insists on five minutes, isn’t being pushy. They’re correcting for a cognitive error the reluctant person can’t see from the inside.</p> <p>2. We are more motivated working together. Partner with someone. Erin hosted a neighborhood gathering in New York City and reflected afterward on what she’d do differently. Her top lesson: “I appreciated the help I did get from neighbors and wished I’d had a co-planner to share more of the work with.”</p> <p>This is consistent with what research finds: People are significantly more likely to initiate and sustain kind and helpful behavior when they’re doing it alongside someone else. A partner doesn’t just make the work easier; they make follow-through more likely, because the social cost of backing out now involves someone else. Several Welcome Committee volunteers named the US Chamber of Connection cohort itself as the thing that got them out the door. Not the training, not the tools, but the fact that others were doing it, too.</p> <p>3. We gain comfort with repeat exposure. Build a rhythm. Hansen has been hosting a monthly porch gathering (coffee, bagels, same spot) for two years. Recently, he watched neighbors spontaneously make plans to go cycling together and quietly organize to look out for a boy on the street whose father is dying of cancer. Neither of those things was planned. They happened because the same people had been attending his events and they had built comfort with each other. Hansen didn’t suggest they help the boy but had created the environment for it to be possible.</p> <p>Research finds that repeated contact with the same faces makes us like and trust them more, independent of what’s said. Those repeated encounters build weak ties, which are how people find help in a crisis, how trust spreads beyond close friends, how a community starts to look out for itself. The first gathering gets you in the door. Showing up again is what builds the neighborhood.</p> <p>What these moments share is spontaneity and clarity of intent. Research finds that unexpected gestures create a positive disruption that formal invitations don’t. They bypass the social calculation people run when a stranger approaches, and they signal warmth without asking for anything back. Research finds that being noticed is the precondition for feeling like you belong.</p> <p>And having a clear role removes the ambiguity that makes first moves feel risky. When Annie said “I’m a Welcome Committee member,” her motives were transparent before she said another word. You don’t need a plan. You need to look up.</p> <p>Giving to others produces more sustained well-being than spending on yourself. The helper’s high is real. Welcoming a newcomer isn’t just a form of service; it’s one of the highest-return social investments you can make.</p> <p>Liz knows this firsthand. The woman who arrived in the Bay Area not knowing a soul, wondering if anyone would notice if she disappeared, is now the person who creates spaces for others to land. “People here took a chance on me,” she says. “So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I want to create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”</p> <p>All friendships begin the same way: by talking to strangers. Someone just has to go first. Years later, Liz became the person who notices.</p> <p>Aaron Hurst is a pioneer social entrepreneur and CEO focused on rebuilding human connection to strengthen communities. He founded the U.S. Chamber of Connection to address the national decline in social ties and trust. Previously, he founded the Taproot Foundation, sparking a $15B pro bono service movement, and led Imperative, which developed purpose profiling tools used by over 200 companies. He’s also co-founder of Board.Dev, connecting tech leaders to nonprofit boards. Author of The Purpose Economy, Aaron’s work has shaped the purpose movement in business and been featured in The New York Times, Bloomberg, and SSIR. He lives in Seattle with his family.</p> <p>Sending reels on social media may seem frivolous or distracting, but it actually functions as a form of relationship maintenance.</p> <p>New research is exploring how our brains translate other people's actions into the experience of feeling loved.</p> <p>Our contributors award our annual "Greater Goodies" to the TV shows that might help you be your best self.</p> <p>Do you embrace a diversity of backgrounds and opinions in others?</p> <p>What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.</p> <p>Discover how writing about our ancestors can strengthen our sense of identity, deepen gratitude, and help us find meaning in our own lives.</p> <p>The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.</p> <p>© 2026 The Greater Good Science Center at the University of California, Berkeley</p> <p style="margin-top: 25px;"> <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/four_ways_to_help_newcomers_feel_like_they_belong" target="_blank" rel="nofollow noopener" style="color: #0d6efd; text-decoration: none; font-weight: bold;"> → Baca artikel asli </a> </p> </div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> </div> </article> <article class="article-card" id="artikel-9659"> <h2>#9659. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://www.spring.org.uk/images/psychopath-6.jpg" alt="What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.</p> <p>Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.</p> <p>Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.</p> <p>This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.</p> <p>The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.</p> <p>Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.</p> <p>Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.</p> <p>The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).</p> <p>The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.</p> <p>In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.</p> <p>The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.</p> <p>Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.</p> <p>Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.</p> <p>Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.</p> <p>People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.</p> <p>The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.</p> <p>Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.</p> <p>There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.</p> <p>One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.</p> <p>For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.</p> <p>Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).</p> <p>Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.</p> <p>Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.</p> <p>Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.</p> <p>It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.</p> <p>Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.</p> <p>That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.</p> <p>The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.</p> <p>Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.</p> <p>All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.</p> <p>This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.</p> <p>Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.</p> <p>Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.</p> <p>The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).</p> <p>Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean</p> <p>Join the free PsyBlog mailing list. Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)</h2> <div class="article-body"> <div style="text-align:center; margin-bottom:20px;"><img src="https://minimalistbaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Cheesy-Vegan-Black-Bean-Enchilada-Skillet-9.jpg" alt="Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy"></div> <div style="text-align:center; margin:20px 0;"> <script type="text/javascript"> atOptions = {'key' : 'f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2','format' : 'iframe','height' : 90,'width' : 728,'params' : {}}; </script> <script type="text/javascript" src="https://upholdbrilliancerecast.com/f9e40eb3b3cd05f1038aac7b36b33ad2/invoke.js"></script> </div> <div class="article-body" style="font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.8; color: #333;"> <p>Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!</p> <p>Everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.</p> <p>This easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!</p> <p>It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.</p> <p>Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!</p> <p>This 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.</p> <p>Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.</p> <p>Next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.</p> <p>And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!</p> <p>We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole new level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).</p> <p>We think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!</p> <p>This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.</p> <p>If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!</p> <p>Tag @minimalistbaker on Instagram and hashtag it #minimalistbaker so we can see all the deliciousness!FacebookTwitterPin It</p> <p>Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!</p> <p>One of the best things I’ve made in a while!! I love how the cheesy sauce solidified on the skillet! 🔥🤤 I subbed the beans for vegan beef and tapioca flour for cornstarch.</p> <p>Whoop! We’re so glad you loved this one, Elizabeth. Thank you for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications! xo</p> <p>Made this tonight for the first time and it was delicious! I’ll be adding this to the dinner menu this winter. I was a bit worried that the cashew cheese was going to be too runny, but sure enough, after adding it to the skillet and covering for 5min, this creamy cheesy goodness was perfect!</p> <p>I didn’t have any corn tortillas, so we left those out and had corn chips on the side. Thank you for this yummy 1-ppt meal!</p> <p>Thank you for the lovely review, Taylor! We’re so glad you enjoyed the recipe and will be adding it into your winter dinner rotation! xo</p> <p>Well that was delightful. Very different for me – my first time buying enchilada sauce. And first time making a cashew cheese. It took more time than indicated – all that fine chopping – but was absolutely delicious. A great one pot meal – thanks!</p> <p>Thank you for sharing your experience, Kate! We’re so happy to hear you enjoyed the dish! Sorry it took longer than expected. xo</p> <p>the “cheese” sauce on top isn’t thickening and is just remaining in a water-like consistency. troubleshooting ideas?</p> <p>Hi! Sorry the hear it’s giving you some trouble. A few ideas: 1) Is it possible the tapioca starch got left out? 2) Is the enchilada layer extra watery? 3) Did you give it a full 5 minutes? You can even keep going past that – it should help. 4) Did you soak your cashews? If so, did you use slightly less water when blending? We hope one of those ideas helps!</p> <p>This was easy and delicious. As the directions say, since my squash was cut a little larger I had to steam longer. I used corn starch instead of tapioca starch and it worked! This one will be on repeat at our house.</p> <p>Thank you for sharing your experience, Alicia! We’re so glad you enjoyed this dish and will be making it again.</p> <p>Yum! I love pizza beans and made it not too long ago.</p> <p>This looks like a nice Mexican twist that is a must-try!</p> <p>It SO is! We’re excited to hear what you think of this one!</p> <p>Yay! We’re so excited to hear what you think, Gina! xo</p> <p>Hi Chana, zucchini will add more moisture which may dilute the flavor, but you could try it! We would suggest chopping it into small cubes and adding in place of the poblano pepper. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>This looks so good! Can you recommend any substitutions for tapioca starch? I have an intolerance.</p> <p>Hi Christine, we would suggest trying arrowroot, or possibly corn starch. Let us know if you try it out!</p> <p>Get our copy of FAN FAVORITES featuring 20 of our most loved, highly-rated recipes!</p> <p>Our FREE 49-Page Fan Favorites e-Book has 20 recipes we think you’ll LOVE!
